lead: Every reading a surveyor takes is an approximation. The tape is a few millimetres long, the bubble sits slightly off centre, the observer reads 4.62 where the mark is at 4.63. This chapter names those imperfections, measures them, and shows how to report a result honestly. You will learn what error and correction mean, why errors are gross, systematic or random, and why accuracy and precision are two different things.
prereq: You need principles and classification of surveying; plane and geodetic for what a survey measures and when earth curvature matters.

blocks.text: The true value is the quantity as it really is: the distance between two pegs, the angle between two lines. Nobody knows it exactly. We adopt a value from a higher-order survey or a calibration certificate and call that the true value X. The observed value x is what the instrument or the surveyor gives.

blocks.where: e is the error, in the same unit as the measurement; x is the observed value; X is the true or accepted value.

blocks.text: A tape reads 100.05 m on a line whose true length is 100.00 m. The error is +0.05 m: the reading is larger than the truth, so the tape is shorter than the length marked on it and it over-reads. A tape that is too long gives readings smaller than the truth.

blocks.where: c is the correction, added to the observed value; e is the error. Here c = −0.05 m.

blocks.text: Sign matters more than anything else here. An error of +0.05 m and a correction of +0.05 m are opposite instructions; using the wrong one puts the answer twice as far from the truth as doing nothing. Tape corrections are built in chain and tape surveying; the accuracy statement of an EDM is in electronic distance measurement (EDM).
Report only the significant figures the instrument supports. A tape read to the nearest centimetre gives 100.03 m, not 100.0300 m.

Gross errors, or blunders, are mistakes: reading 4.62 as 4.92, booking a backsight in the foresight column, dropping a whole 30 m tape length. They are large, one-off and unpredictable, and statistics cannot find them. Only checks can: measure from both ends, add the parts and compare with the whole, keep a second observer. A suspected blunder is rejected and the measurement repeated.

Systematic errors repeat with the same sign and about the same size under the same conditions. They push every reading the same way, so they bias the result. A steel tape standardised at 20 °C and used at 38 °C reads short on every span of the day. They come in three groups.

items: Instrumental: the tape is too long or too short, its zero mark is worn, an EDM carries a constant offset, a level bubble is out of adjustment.
Personal: the eye is not square to the scale (parallax), the bubble is judged centred when it is not, one observer always reads a little late.
Natural: temperature, humidity and pressure of the air, refraction, and wind.

blocks.text: Because the sign and size repeat, averaging does not remove a systematic error. It must be measured by standardising the tape against a known baseline and taken out by a correction: standardisation, temperature, tension, sag, slope and alignment for taping; constant plus parts per million for an EDM.

Random errors are the small scatter in any reading: the bubble never sits in exactly the same place, the pull on the tape is not steady, the mark is estimated to the nearest half millimetre. Their sign and size cannot be predicted, but over many readings they partly cancel — repeating is the cure for random error and no cure at all for bias.
Accuracy is how close a measured value, or the mean of a set, lies to the true value. Precision is how close repeated readings lie to one another. Accuracy is about bias; precision is about scatter.

Readings of 100.02, 100.04, 100.03, 100.05 and 100.01 m on a line of true length 100.00 m are precise: they span 4 cm from lowest to highest and their standard deviation is about 1.6 cm. They are not accurate: every one lies above the truth, a systematic error of about +0.03 m. A single reading of 100.00 m from a carelessly held tape is accurate by luck and not precise at all. Four combinations exist: accurate and precise (the goal), precise but not accurate (calibrate and correct), accurate but not precise (repeat and average), neither (start again).
Three numbers describe a set of n repeated readings x₁ to xₙ.

blocks.where: x̄ (x-bar) is the mean, in m; n is the number of readings.
dᵢ is the deviation of reading i from the mean, in m. The deviations of a set always add to zero.

s is the sample standard deviation, in m; Σdᵢ² is the sum of squared deviations, in m²; n − 1 is used because the mean already used one piece of information. The uncertainty of the mean is about s/√n, so four times as many readings halve it.

blocks.text: Results built from measurements carry their errors along. For a sum or difference the absolute errors combine in quadrature; for a product or quotient the relative errors do.
S = a ± b:  e<sub>S</sub> = √(e<sub>a</sub>² + e<sub>b</sub>²)    P = a × b or a ÷ b:  e<sub>P</sub>/P = √((e<sub>a</sub>/a)² + (e<sub>b</sub>/b)²)
blocks.where: e<sub>a</sub> and e<sub>b</sub> are the errors of a and b; e<sub>S</sub> is the error of the sum; e<sub>P</sub> is the error of the product. Both assume the errors are independent and random.

figure.caption: The five readings sit close together (s = 0.016 m) but all lie above the true 100.00 m; their mean is 0.03 m high. The set is precise but not accurate, and the bias must be found by calibration and removed by a correction.

spec.aria: A number line from 99.98 to 100.07 metres with the true value at 100.00, five readings from 100.01 to 100.05, their mean at 100.03 with a band of one standard deviation, and an arrow showing the bias of 0.03 metres.

examples.question: A distance is measured five times: 100.02, 100.04, 100.03, 100.05 and 100.01 m. The true value is 100.00 m. Find the mean, the error of the mean, and the sample standard deviation. State whether the set is accurate, precise, or both.
steps: Error of the mean: e = 100.03 − 100.00 = +0.03 m, so the correction is c = −0.03 m.
Deviations from the mean: −0.01, +0.01, 0.00, +0.02, −0.02 m. They add to zero, as a check. Their squares: 0.0001, 0.0001, 0.0000, 0.0004, 0.0004 m², so Σdᵢ² = 0.0010 m².
Uncertainty of the mean: s/√n = 0.016 / √5 = 0.007 m. The bias of 0.03 m is about four times this, so the set is precise but not accurate: a systematic error dominates.
examples.answer: Mean = 100.03 m, error of the mean = +0.03 m (correction −0.03 m), sample standard deviation = 0.016 m; the set is precise but not accurate.
examples.check:
xs = [100.02, 100.04, 100.03, 100.05, 100.01]
true = 100.00
n = len(xs)
mean = sum(xs) / n
err = mean - true
devs = [x - mean for x in xs]
ss = sum(d * d for d in devs)
var = ss / (n - 1)
sd = var ** 0.5
print(round(mean, 2))
print(round(err, 2))
print(round(sd, 3))

traps: Correction is the negative of the error. Adding the error instead of subtracting it doubles the mistake — a favourite one-mark deduction.
Low scatter is not proof of correctness: in the worked example the readings are tight but the mean is 30 mm high.
Averaging kills random error, not systematic error. More readings shrink s/√n and leave the bias untouched.
Dividing Σdᵢ² by n instead of n − 1 makes s too small; and the squares are in m², so the standard deviation comes back in m.
A blunder is rejected and re-measured, never averaged in.

quiz.q: Define accuracy and precision as used in surveying.
quiz.a: Accuracy is the closeness of a measured value, or the mean of a set, to the true value. Precision is the closeness of repeated readings to one another, that is, small scatter.

quiz.q: A 30 m steel tape is 8 mm too long. Twenty readings of a line are averaged. Does the mean become closer to the truth? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The tape error is systematic: every reading is short by 8 mm per tape length, so the bias stays in the mean. Averaging only reduces random scatter, roughly as s/√n. The tape must be standardised and a correction applied.

quiz.q: A line measures 250.06 m and its accepted true value is 250.00 m. Find the error and the correction.
quiz.a: e = 250.06 − 250.00 = +0.06 m. c = −e = −0.06 m, added to the observed value to recover 250.00 m.

quiz.q: Four readings of a line are 50.01, 50.03, 50.02 and 50.02 m. Find the mean and the sample standard deviation.
Six readings of a baseline give a mean of 500.08 m and s = 0.004 m; the true value is 500.00 m. Comment on accuracy and precision, and state what to do next.
quiz.a: 4 mm scatter is small, so the set is precise. The mean is 80 mm high, a systematic error about fifty times the uncertainty of the mean, s/√6 = 0.0016 m. It is not accurate. Calibrate the instrument and apply a correction; extra readings will not help.

quiz.q: Classify each error: (a) the worn zero end of a tape is used as the start mark; (b) a steel tape used at 40 °C; (c) the bubble is judged centred but is not; (d) gusty wind along the line.
quiz.a: (a) systematic, instrumental: the worn zero mark adds a constant offset to every reading; correct it by starting from a sound graduation (for example the 1 m mark) or by applying the tape's standardisation correction. (b) systematic, natural (temperature, corrected by the temperature formula). (c) systematic, personal (parallax and judgement). (d) random, with a natural cause — partly cancels over repeats.

quiz.q: Two parts of a line, 40.00 m with error ±0.02 m and 60.00 m with error ±0.03 m, are measured separately and added. Find the error of the total.
quiz.a: e<sub>S</sub> = √(0.02² + 0.03²) = √(0.0004 + 0.0009) = √0.0013 = 0.036 m, so the total length is 100.00 ± 0.036 m (about ±0.04 m if rounded to two decimals).

beyond: Not for the exam. A survey firm quotes an EDM as a constant plus parts per million, and checks instruments on a calibrated baseline. GNSS work adds its own error budget — satellite clock and orbit, ionosphere and troposphere, multipath, and satellite geometry expressed as DOP — which is taught with GNSS in modern surveying. Least-squares adjustment, the general machine for combining many observations of unequal weight, comes with control surveys (weights and adjustment of observations).
